attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, said in his own voice.

semantics.note: The universal 'without exception' scope is kept. The 'no solution' half is untestable, and the contract rightly leaves it out of the verdict.

contract.note: Reading 'margins' as gross margin and using 2025 up to the post date are ordinary choices for 'are improving', and both are flagged. Since the claim is universal, one credible counterexample is enough to contradict it.

evidence.note: Sourced report, available before the evaluation date: Cursor went from negative to slightly positive gross margin, which the report ties to the November 2025 Composer model. The exact month it turned positive is unclear ('until recently').
Analyst estimate: Replit's gross margin rose from -14% in April 2025 to 23% in July 2025, inside the period.
Replit's margins swung between -14% and 36% in 2025. That tempers how lasting the gain was, but it doesn't show margins were flat or falling.
The CEO's own unverified claim that Replit is gross-margin positive. This is a company disclosure.

reviews.rationale: The claim says no AI startup was improving its margins. Two estimates contradict it: Replit's estimated gross margin went from -14% to 23% in mid-2025, and Cursor moved from negative to positive gross margin after November 2025. Both are estimates, not audited figures, but one credible counterexample is enough. The 'no solution' part isn't graded.

attribution.note: Zitron's own argument and arithmetic. He quotes the CFO's figure only as the thing he is comparing against.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'exceeding', the over-$6B sum and the 'I believe' hedge. The hedged inference is graded only through the firm claim that the numbers don't match.

contract.note: 'Exceeding $5B' is only a floor, so the contract tests his point against actual cumulative revenue from the S-1. That fairly captures his claim that the run-rates outran real revenue. The result depends on this framing, which is flagged.

evidence.note: The CFO's 'exceeding $5 billion to date', the figure he compares against. It gives no cut-off date.
Audited revenue for 2023–2025 totals about $5.01B, which matches the declaration as a count through year-end 2025.
Q4 2025 revenue (about $680M a month) roughly matches the December run-rate. Q1 2026 brought in $4.73B, so lifetime revenue by early March was well above $6B. Quarterly figures are unaudited.
The run-rate definition in the S-1 is a conventional annualization. It is a company disclosure dated October 2026 and doesn't confirm the method behind earlier press figures.
Third-party record of his roughly $6.66B sum. It restates the speaker's claim and isn't proof of anything.

reviews.rationale: The S-1 shows about $5.01B of revenue through year-end 2025, consistent with the CFO's figure. It also shows $4.73B more in Q1 2026, so actual revenue by early March was above the over-$6B his run-rate sum implied. Q4 2025 revenue roughly matched the December run-rate. The mismatch he claims, and the 'new definition' he infers from it, don't hold.

semantics.note: The drafter adds 'of funding', a meaning the speaker never gave the $30B. The line is rhetorical shorthand plus a value judgment ('bad business'), not a checkable observation.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to pick a meaning for the $30B, which would decide the result without support in his words. 'Bad business' is normative.

evidence.note: The filing gives more than $60B raised and over $10B spent on training and inference. Neither matches $30B.
2023–2025 operating expenses total about $16.6B against about $5.0B of revenue, which also doesn't match $30B.

reviews.rationale: The $30B has no stated meaning. It could be one funding round, total funding or total spending, and the filing matches none of them. 'Bad business' is a value judgment. The claim can't be scored without inventing a reading the speaker didn't give.

attribution.note: His own aside, written in his own voice. The Blackstone detail comes from reporting, but the affordability claim is his.

semantics.note: The proposition faithfully isolates his present-tense claim that OpenAI cannot afford the Oracle compute.

contract.note: Counting financing as part of 'afford' is an ordinary reading, though he may have meant from revenue alone. Both readings are flagged. Most payments fall due from 2027, so what counts as 'afford' shapes the result.

evidence.note: The $300B Oracle contract begins in 2027, so most payments come after the post.
About $110B in committed funding in February 2026, which weighs against near-term inability to pay. It doesn't show what payments were due or made.
FT-reported projection that OpenAI's funding runs out by 2028. It's about future affordability, not a missed payment.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no payment schedule, no missed or renegotiated payment, and no confirmation that payments due were made. Large committed funding weighs against inability to pay in the near term. Most of the obligations start in 2027, and projections suggest funding gaps later on. The evidence doesn't settle the claim either way.
